But it tells the buyer: “This wasn’t really worth what you said.” Over the customer lifetime, that one move can cost: £10K+ in missed expansion Renewal delays Referral silence Team-wide pricing confidence If your team is defaulting to price before value, the system, not the rep, is broken.

items.title: Why are you paying for your customers to churn?
items.quote: Why are you paying for your customers to churn? You’re not just losing customers. You’re funding their exit. Acquisition spend: gone Onboarding time: sunk Expansion potential: vanished And what did you learn when they left? Usually ... nothing. Because most churn isn’t a CS issue. It’s a trust system failure that started before the contract was signed. If your renewals feel like uphill battles, it’s worth asking: Are you building loyalty, or just prolonging the loss?

items.title: 1. Open strong
items.quote: 1. Open strong You’ve got seconds to earn attention. Great comics start hot. So should you. Ditch the preamble.

items.title: 2. Read the room
items.quote: 2. Read the room Comics watch for tiny shifts in energy. Great sellers notice when buying signals dry up, or when someone tunes out. You can't sell if you're not paying attention.

items.title: 3. Earn the right to challenge
items.quote: 3. Earn the right to challenge The best comics don’t start with taboo jokes, they build trust first. Same in sales. Build credibility then go deeper.

items.title: 4. Move on fast
items.quote: 4. Move on fast If a joke flops, they don’t explain it, they let it go. Same with prospects who aren't a fit. Don't waste energy trying to revive the dead.

items.title: 5. Use silence well
items.quote: 5. Use silence well Amateurs panic in the quiet. Pros use it to build tension and make people lean in. Learn to shut up at the right moment.

items.title: 6. Cut the fat
items.quote: 6. Cut the fat Every word in a set is intentional. Your pitch, email, or deck should be too. Say less. Say it better.

items.title: 7. Practise in the wild
items.quote: 7. Practise in the wild Comics test material live and tweak it constantly. Sellers should do the same. You don’t get better in your head. So yes, I’m off to Edinburgh again this year. items.title: 1. The Question That Won’t Go Away

tags.label: employees hesitating to tell the truth

items.quote: 1. The Question That Won’t Go Away Every leader swears they value trust. So why do their people hold their breath when they walk into the room? Maybe trust isn’t built. Maybe it’s remembered, until the moment we forget how to earn it. You can buy compliance. You can rent attention. You can’t force conviction. When was the last time someone told you the truth before you asked for it? And why did they hesitate?

items.title: 2. The Physics of Absence
items.quote: 2. The Physics of Absence You don’t notice trust when it’s present. You notice it when it leaves, like oxygen, or light, or sound after an explosion. Silence doesn’t mean safety. It means calculation. How many decisions are made every day by people deciding what not to say? What does that cost in time, energy, margin? Who’s keeping that score?

items.title: 3. The Weight in the Room
items.quote: 3. The Weight in the Room Look around your next meeting. Watch for the glance before someone speaks. Watch how long it takes to exhale after a question. That pause is the tax you pay for every time trust was broken and never repaired. Do you call that professionalism? Or fear with good posture?

items.title: 4. The Substitutes We Invent
items.quote: 4. The Substitutes We Invent When trust thins, control thickens. We add process. We chase visibility. We mistake proof for progress. Why does a culture that claims transparency hide behind metrics? Dashboards multiply. Reports replace conversation. Everyone is accountable and no one feels responsible. When did evidence become a weapon instead of a mirror?

items.title: 5. The Small Mechanics of Distrust
items.quote: 5. The Small Mechanics of Distrust It starts with tone. Then with timing. Then with who gets copied in on the email. Tiny edits. Tiny hesitations. Tiny withdrawals of faith. None of them hurt by themselves. Together, they make gravity heavier. How many grams of distrust does it take to ground a company?

items.title: 6. The Experiment
items.quote: 6. The Experiment Try this: In your next one-to-one, start with, “I might be missing something - What do you see that I don’t?” Then hold your tongue long enough for honesty to find its way out. Do they fill the silence with truth or performance? And what does that tell you about how safe they feel with you?

items.title: 7. The Recovery Loop
items.quote: 7. The Recovery Loop Trust doesn’t come back with time. It comes back with witness. One apology made before it’s demanded. One small promise kept where everyone can see it. One leader who says, “We stopped listening. Let’s start there.” Who has to go first this time? And what would happen if it was you?

items.title: 8. The Cost Curve
items.quote: 8. The Cost Curve Fear burns cash to stay busy. Trust compounds value while you sleep. The numbers are easy. The question isn’t. If fear costs so much, why do you keep buying it?

items.title: 9. The Unfinished Line
items.quote: 9. The Unfinished Line Maybe trust isn’t what keeps the system human. Maybe it’s what keeps YOU human inside the system. But if that’s true, what happens the next time you trade honesty for harmony? And what will it cost when you realise the harmony was never real? Don’t rush to agree Test it. items.title: Strategy is what you’re willing to ignore

items.title: Removing constraints to unlock high performance
items.quote: The business doesn’t need more goals - it needs fewer constraints. Rules protect mediocrity. They give safety to people who stopped thinking. High performers don’t just need tighter systems. They need clearer direction and fewer walls. When everything’s over-structured, initiative dies quietly. Remove the rules. Keep the standards. Then watch how fast people rise. Which rule would you delete if you trusted your team completely?

items.title: The real job of a founder is clarity, not growth

You don’t need to move more. You need to see better. Take a Peek in the Mirror: What problem would disappear tomorrow if you saw it clearly today?

items.title: You don’t need another framework, you need one real decision

tags.label: over-relying on frameworks and models instead of choosing

items.quote: You don’t need another framework. You need one real decision. You’ve read the books. Bought the course. Filled the whiteboard ... twice. Every new model feels like momentum. But it’s just motion. Because frameworks let you think about the work instead of doing the hard part ... choosing. You don’t have a strategy problem. You have a courage problem. Burnout isn’t from doing too much. It’s from never deciding what to stop. Clarity isn’t found in frameworks. It’s found in finally choosing.

items.title: Building a business that scales while remaining human
items.quote: I built a business that worked. But I didn’t. Revenue was up. Team was growing. Clients were happy. And I was done. Tired in a way sleep couldn’t fix. Because I built the company I thought I should - not the one I actually wanted. Success without peace isn’t success. It’s survival. I had to rebuild the business around a version of me that could breathe again. Now the goal’s simpler: Build something that scales ... and still leaves you human.

items.title: Culture is what you tolerate, not perks

tags.label: standards slipping due to fear of conflict

items.quote: I thought culture was about perks. Friday beers. Ping pong. “We’re a family.” But culture isn’t what you bribe people with. It’s what you tolerate when no one’s watching. We had fun ... but we avoided truth. We praised effort over output. We confused kindness with comfort. When standards slipped, I called it “learning.” It was actually fear - fear of being the bad guy. The day I started protecting performance, people started respecting the culture. Perks fade. ... Standards scale.

items.title: Hiring for Judgment and Direction Over Energy and Speed

tags.label: team moving fast into the wrong direction

items.quote: I hired for energy, not judgment. I wanted momentum - people who could “move fast.” And they did. Straight into the wrong fires. Everything looked busy. Nothing was moving forward. Turns out speed without sense just burns fuel. I didn’t need more energy. I needed better judgment. The team that changed everything wasn’t the loudest - they were the calmest. One of the easiest mistakes in sales management is trying to manufacture urgency through pressure instead of finding it in the buyer's world. End of month pushes. Expiring discounts. Quarter end pressure disguised as help. Managers call this creating momentum. Buyers feel exposed. A buyer's real job is to decide without being punished for thinking. They need room to compare options. They need time to test regret.

Peers managing exposure. Functions reducing risk. Quiet vetoes with no calendar invite. The person you call the decision-maker is usually a representative, not the authority.
